title: The task
subtitle: what the lander senses, does, and is scored on

transcript.text: Lesson one. The task. Before we evolve anything, let's look closely at the problem our pilot has to solve.

This is Lunar Lander, a small physics game from the Gymnasium library. The lander starts near the top of the screen with a random push, and it has to touch down softly on the pad between the two flags. Many times a second, the lander senses eight numbers. Its position, across and up. Its speed, across and up. Its tilt, and how fast it is spinning. And two switches that turn on when a leg touches the ground. With those eight numbers, it picks one of four actions. Do nothing. Fire the left engine. Fire the main engine underneath. Or fire the right engine. The side engines push the lander sideways and spin it, and the main engine pushes it up.

The game keeps score while it flies. Moving toward the pad, slowing down, and staying level all earn a little. Drifting away, speeding up, and tilting all cost a little. There are bigger events too. Each leg that touches the ground earns ten points. Coming to rest earns a hundred. Crashing costs a hundred. And fuel isn't free. Every frame the main engine fires costs a third of a point. The side engines cost a tenth as much. Add it all up over one flight. A score of two hundred or more counts as solved.
Lesson two. The controller. How can thirty-six numbers fly a spacecraft?

Our pilot is one small table of numbers, called a matrix. Each of the eight inputs is multiplied by four weights, one for each action. Then a bias is added to each total. That gives four scores. Whichever score is highest, that action fires. Watch the scores on the right change as the lander flies, and the winning action change with them. Eight inputs times four actions is thirty-two weights. Add four biases, and you have thirty-six numbers. That is the entire pilot.

Let's learn to read the table. Each row is one input, and each column is one action. Orange cells are positive weights, and blue cells are negative. The brighter the cell, the bigger the number. Read across a row, and you see how one input votes. Horizontal speed pushes some actions up and others down, all at the same time. Read down a column, and you see everything that argues for one action. This is the left engine's column. A single cell is a single rule. A positive weight means the bigger this input, the more I want this action. A negative weight means the opposite. Here: drifting right is a strong vote for the left engine. The last row is the bias. It's a head start, or a handicap, that each action gets, whatever the state.

Now let's watch one real decision. Each input is multiplied by its weight, and the products are added up in each column. The lander is falling fast, so the falling speed pushes the main engine's score up. It has the highest total, so the main engine fires.

title: Population and fitness
subtitle: many candidates, and a way to rank them

transcript.text: Lesson three. Population and fitness. Evolution needs two things. Many candidates, and a way to tell the good ones from the bad.

We start with a population of pilots. Each one is thirty-six random numbers. In training there are fifty of them. Here are eighteen. Each pilot flies, and we score it. With random numbers, every one of them crashes. But some crash later, or closer to the pad, and that difference is all evolution needs. We keep the best half, and the rest are thrown away. The survivors decide where the next generation will be sampled.

So what is the score? Each pilot flies ten different episodes, each with its own terrain and starting push. Then we combine three things. First, the average reward from the game itself. That already rewards approaching the pad, and it punishes crashing and wasted fuel. Second, a bonus of a hundred points, times the share of episodes that end in a landing. Landing is what we really want, so it's worth a lot. Third, a small speed bonus, up to thirty points, for landing quickly. It is multiplied by the landing rate, so a pilot can't earn it by crashing fast.

title: Inside CMA-ES
subtitle: how the search decides where to look next

transcript.text: Lesson four. Inside CMA-ES. How does the algorithm decide where to look next?
Every generation runs the same loop. Sample new pilots. Fly them. Rank them. Then update, and repeat. The algorithm never looks inside the pilot. It only sees the scores.

The new pilots are drawn from a cloud, a bell-shaped distribution over all thirty-six numbers. It has three parts. The mean is the centre of the cloud. It's the algorithm's current best guess for a good pilot. The step size, sigma, sets how far from the mean new candidates land. Big steps explore. Small steps fine-tune. And the covariance sets the shape. It lets the cloud stretch in the directions where good pilots were found, and stay narrow everywhere else. In our problem the cloud has thirty-six dimensions, one per weight. To watch it work, let's shrink it down to two.

Here is a toy problem with two numbers. Dark means low cost, which is good, and bright means high cost. The green cross is the best answer, but the algorithm doesn't know where it is. Each generation, it samples twelve points and keeps the best six, shown in orange. It moves the mean toward them, and reshapes the ellipse to follow the direction the winners came from. Watch the cloud stretch along the valley and race down it. As it closes in, the step size shrinks, until it settles on the answer. Learning that shape is what the name means: covariance matrix adaptation.
Lesson five. Generations. Now let's watch the population improve, one generation at a time.

Each dot is one pilot. Each column is one generation of fifty pilots, and the height of a dot is its fitness. Red pilots mostly crash, and green ones mostly land. In the first thirty generations, nearly every pilot crashes. But each generation is sampled around the best of the last one, so the whole column creeps upward. The best pilot lands half its episodes by generation thirty-two. Then the whole population climbs. By generation fifty, a fifth of the pilots land. By seventy-five, most of them do. The orange line is the best pilot, and the blue line is the average. As the population agrees on one strategy, the average catches up with the best.

Fitness is just a number, so let's watch the flights. Every pilot of a generation starts from exactly the same spot, with the same push, and we draw where each one goes. Generation zero is chaos. Pilots fall straight down, or fire an engine and fly off the screen. One generation later, and then five, the paths change shape, but not one of them lands yet. By generation ten, a few paths bend toward the pad. Through twenty and thirty, the paths tighten, but only a handful land. By forty, eight land. And by fifty, nineteen of the fifty pilots land. By seventy-five, forty land. By one hundred, forty-eight. In the end, the trails bundle into one smooth curve between the flags.

This is the same population, seen as points. Each pilot is thirty-six numbers. A method called principal component analysis flattens them down to two, so each dot is a whole pilot. The centre of the cloud, in blue, travels a long way from where it started, toward the region where pilots land. The white line is its path. Here is a neat trick. Only the highest score matters, so if you double every weight, every decision stays the same. As the weights grow, the same step size becomes a smaller and smaller step relative to them. The search turns into fine-tuning on its own.

title: Evolution in flight
subtitle: the best pilot along the way

transcript.text: Lesson six. Evolution in flight. What does the best pilot look like along the way?

Here is the best pilot from different points in training, all facing the same start. A random pilot, then the champions of generations ten, thirty, sixty and one hundred, and the final best. The random pilot fires its main engine without a break, and flies away. The champion of generation ten fires its engines, but still crashes. By generation thirty, the best pilot lands. Later champions land too, with steadier and more efficient flights.

Here is the centre of the population, drawn as the weight matrix itself. The colours are scaled to the biggest weight in each generation, so we can see the pattern while it forms. At generation zero it is noise. The strongest rules in the end are all about speed. Drifting right fires the left engine. Falling fires the main engine, and stops the lander from doing nothing. Spinning clockwise fires the left engine too.
Lesson seven. Reading the weights. Because the pilot is linear, we can understand exactly what it learned. Let's take it apart.

Start with one decision. The lander is high up and falling fast. Each input is multiplied by its weight, and the products are added up per action. The falling speed alone gives the main engine a big push, and takes a lot away from do nothing. The main engine wins. A few frames earlier, the lander was tilted to the right. Now it's close. The tilt and the height add votes to the left engine, and it wins by a small margin. Firing it turns the lander back upright. Near the ground, the lander is spinning to the left. Spin has the biggest weight of all, on the left engine, and here it counts against it. The left engine drops far behind, and the right engine wins. That spins the lander back.

But be careful. A big weight doesn't always mean a big effect. Here are the sizes of all the weights. What also matters is how much each input actually changes in flight. Altitude moves a lot. Spin barely moves at all, so its large weights are multiplied by small numbers. The legs are always zero in the air. Multiply the two, and you get the influence of each weight. The three that matter most are drift on the left engine, and falling speed on do nothing and on the main engine.

We can also draw a rule as a map. Across is the tilt, and up and down is the spin, with every other input held at a typical value. Each colour is the action the pilot would choose there. The white line is a real flight. It stays near the middle, where the colours meet, so the pilot hops between engines with every small change.

Here's a second map. Across is the height, and up and down is the falling speed. Falling fast, it fires the main engine. Falling slowly while still high up, it uses the side engines. And close to the ground, moving slowly, it does nothing. The real flight zig-zags along the border. The pilot brakes just enough, again and again, all the way down.

Now let's put it together, one action at a time. The main engine fires when the lander is falling. Its bias is negative, so it stays off unless the fall is fast enough. Do nothing gets a strong vote when the lander is rising, and a strong vote against it when the left leg is down. This pilot almost never just waits. The left engine fixes drift and spin. It fires when the lander drifts right, or spins clockwise, and it pushes the lander back. And the right engine is the default. It fires almost half the time, in small, cheap pulses, whenever no other rule wins. There's no rule for drifting left. When that happens, the left engine loses its votes, and the right engine wins by default.

Finally, let's test which weights the pilot really needs. We set one weight to zero, fly thirty episodes, and see how many still land. Then we put it back, and try the next one. Most weights can go with little harm. But remove the rule that links falling speed to the main engine, and not a single flight lands. Without it, the pilot never brakes, and simply falls.
